hook.text: A coach screams at players after a terrible game. Next game, they improve. Proof that yelling works?

buildup.text: Extreme performances tend to be followed by more average ones. This is regression to the mean — a statistical fact.

discovery.text: The regression fallacy: mistaking this natural statistical tendency for the effect of an intervention.

twist.text: Sports Illustrated cover jinx, sophomore slumps, miracle cures after worst days — all regression to the mean.

climax.text: Without a control group, you can't distinguish intervention effects from natural regression.

punchline.text: After your worst day, tomorrow is probably better anyway.

quiz.question: What is the regression fallacy?
options: Believing that society is getting worse
Mistaking regression to the mean for an intervention's effect

details.summary: The regression fallacy attributes a statistical regression toward the mean to a causal intervention. Extreme performance naturally returns toward average, but people credit whatever happened between the extreme and the return.
details.whyItMatters: This fallacy makes useless interventions seem effective and punishes people for normal statistical variation, distorting everything from coaching to medicine.
takeaways: Extreme values naturally regress toward the average
Interventions applied after extreme events get false credit
Understanding regression to the mean prevents superstitious beliefs

faq.question: What is a common example of the regression fallacy in everyday life?
faq.answer: A team performs terribly one week, the coach gives an angry speech, and they improve the next week. The coach gets credit, but the team likely would have improved anyway because extreme bad performance naturally regresses toward the average.

faq.question: How does regression to the mean affect beliefs about alternative medicine?
faq.answer: People seek alternative treatments when symptoms are at their worst. Symptoms naturally fluctuate and tend to improve from extreme lows. The alternative treatment gets credit for the natural regression, creating a false causal belief.
